newsitem.title: FRANCE: Channel tunnel faces lenghty disruption after fire.
newsitem.headline: Channel tunnel faces lenghty disruption after fire.

text.p: Eurotunnel still hopes to restart passenger trains through the Channel Tunnel on Wednesday but inspection has shown that fire damage is worse than first thought.

The Anglo-French link could face weeks of disruption after a blaze on a lorry aboard a freight train -- the first major accident since it opened two years ago -- injured eight people and damaged 600 metres (yards) of the 51-km (32-mile) rail tunnel.
"There is a lot of mess down there," Alain Bertrand, operations director of Eurotunnel SA Plc told Britain's Press Association news agency in Calais.

"Our people will be working throughout the night but I think we have to be less optimistic than we were earlier. Clearly there is more to do to restore services and equipment which were damaged by the fire."

With one of the two main tunnels undamaged, hopes had been high earlier on Tuesday that, a partial service could begin on Wednesday morning. Bertrand said some travellers may be allowed through on Wednesday afternoon "at the very earliest".
When Eurostar high-speed trains do start running again the best the company can hope for is a quarter to a third of normal traffic.

Shuttle services for cars -- which, like trucks, are loaded aboard trains at Calais or Folkestone -- would take second place. The tunnel comprises three parallel tunnels -- two for trains, one for maintenance and emergencies.

French state railway company SNCF said it was not sure when traffic could resume and urged Eurostar passengers with bookings for Wednesday to postpone their trip. Those who turned up would be put on ferries, the tunnel's arch-rivals.
The fire started in one of 29 trucks aboard a shuttle train and about 70 French and British fire-fighters fought all night to control it, 18 kms (11 miles) from the French entrance.
The 31 truck drivers and three train crew were evacuated suffering from the effects of toxic fumes and eight needed hospital treatment.

The blaze was a new setback for the troubled Eurotunnel operator which is trying to shake off a record of breakdowns, cost over-runs and debts and recently came close to bankruptcy after restructuring its $15 billion debt.
Rails, electric cables, carriages and 15 trucks were damaged. Eurotunnel said the cost of repairs was not yet known.
British Transport Secretary Sir George Young told parliament the Channel Tunnel Safety Authority would have to scrutinise the design of freight trains.
Any change in the design would be another costly blow to Eurotunnel which also faces heavy costs from reduced traffic .

Its shares, which peaked at 130 francs ($25.50) in 1989 on optimism for the first link between Britain and mainland Europe since the Ice Age, closed 0.10 franc (20 cents) down at 7.70 ($1.50) in Paris on Tuesday.
The stricken freight train has been uncoupled and the operational part taken to the British end in Folkestone, 50 miles (75 km) south of London.
The damaged section is due to be towed out on the French side to Calais, but Bertrand said it was too early to say when that would happen.
A lot will depend on whether the rolling stock can still roll after the intense heat of a blaze which is believed to have fused some of the fittings to the track.
Bertrand said one of the main lines of inquiry would be a suggestion that a lorry's cargo was already smouldering before the freight train entered the tunnel at Calais.
"We are looking into that. It may be there were the beginnings of a fire early on which our fire alarms did not detect," he said.
"It might have been that it did not become a big fire until the train was inside the tunnel."

Bertrand insisted that the first inspection of the damage had done nothing to change Eurotunnel's belief that security precautions and evacuation tactics fulfilled the promise of pre-launch exercises.
